cards.source_text: - Using satellite data and water samples taken by ships over the last 40 years, researchers employed machine learning to untangle the history of marine heat waves hitting simultaneously with acidification events. - They found that these compound events happen more frequently than would be expected by chance, attributing them to ocean physics that allow marine heat waves to become unusually acidic in some regions. - The resulting database captured some “double-hit” heat-acidity events that have been largely ignored in the scientific literature, such as a massive 2016 event in the Southern Pacific Ocean that lasted eight months. - Experts say more research is urgently needed to better understand how these compound events affect marine life and fisheries. Between 2014 and 2015, a marine heatwave known as “The Blob” warmed an area of the Pacific Ocean larger than the United States and Mexico combined. The massive event fueled toxic algae blooms, collapsed fisheries, killed off millions of emaciated seabirds, sent dead fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and sea otters washing up on Alaska and British Columbia coasts, and dotted California shores with starving sea lions. Though best known as a marine heat wave, The Blob was also an extreme acidification event. Yet occurrences of these compound heat-acidity extreme events remain poorly understood. A new study, published in the journal AGU Advances in August, provides a detailed look at the frequency, intensity and duration of these compound events during the last four decades. The study reveals an understudied aspect of marine heat waves that could have implications for the developing 2026-2027 “super” El Niño, in which waters in the equatorial Pacific become unusually warm due to changing wind patterns. Researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zurich) found compound heat-acidity events across the globe happen together “more frequently than would be expected by chance,” they wrote. Instead, the researchers attributed their occurrence to underlying ocean physics that allow marine heat waves to become unusually acidic in some regions. cards.source_text: Sebastian Thrun, a computer scientist, entrepreneur, and adjunct professor at Stanford University (whose projects have included Waymo, Google X, Google Street View, and more) has launched a study to evaluate “the capabilities and limitations of AI systems for writing English-language philosophy.” Called PhilosophyBench, the study is focused on “whether AI can generate novel philosophical ideas and develop them clearly with depth and sophistication, not merely summarize existing views or apply existing philosophical theories.” The advisory board for the study includes philosophers Ned Block, Nancy Cartwright Ruth Chang, Kit Fine, Gideon Rosen, Jonathan Schaffer, Crispin Wright, and Linda Zagzebski, as well as computer scientists. The project involves developing “an independent academic benchmark against which claims about capabilities in AI philosophical reasoning and writing can be evaluated. If a new AI model comes out and claims are made about its philosophical capabilities, we hope that this study will provide an independent methodology that can judge those claims.” The questions to be addressed by the project include (according to its FAQ): - Can an AI generate novel philosophical ideas and develop them clearly with depth and sophistication? - Can an AI generate essays that could be accepted to a philosophy journal, or earn admission to a leading philosophy PhD program? - To what extent does providing human philosophy BAs and PhDs access to AI tools change the quality of the philosophical writing that they produce (this is called an “uplift” study)? - Given that many frontier AI models are already pre-trained on an extensive set of philosophical work across human history, what limitations, if any, prevent frontier AI models from producing philosophical work at the quality level of the best philosophical work in human history? - When AIs write philosophy, are there any patterns in how they write that reveal anything about AI alignment, particularly when AIs are asked to produce novel arguments? - What, if anything, might the philosophical capabilities of current AI systems tell us about how future AI systems might develop? The project is currently looking for people with philosophical training to help with the project (“professional philosophers, graduate students, or advanced philosophy undergraduates, as demonstrated through formal education or other appropriate evidence”). Further details are at the PhilosophyBench site.
cards.source_title: New Study on AI’s Philosophical Skills

Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them. I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile. cards.source_text: Critical theorists like Theodor Adorno may have overreached in claiming that all mass culture is mediocre, mechanized propaganda made to justify the status quo. But that doesn’t mean they were entirely wrong. Over and over we see even the most subversive art, literature, film, and music has a way of being tamed and Bowdlerized. Global mega-corporate industries don’t need to censor what they don’t like; they only need to buy it, rebrand it, or price it out of reach. So what? Why do we need challenging, independent art when we have endless entertainment? Is the concept a nostalgic, elitist, Eurocentric idea? Artists have justified the need for art since antiquity, with poetic and logical arguments of every kind. But Dada artists of the early 20th century broke ranks, building their movement on the insight that no defense could possibly mean anything when it came to art’s purpose, especially in the face of the technocratic slaughter of World War I. When the hyperrationalism of modernity led to mass death and destruction, the only humane response was to declare war on rationalization—to “destroy the hoaxes of reason,” as French artist Jean Arp put it. “For the disillusioned artists of the Dada movement,” the Museum of Modern Art explains, “the war merely confirmed the degradation of social structures that led to such violence: corrupt and nationalist politics, repressive social values, and unquestioning conformity of culture and thought.” Dada took a combative stance against, for one thing, the insistence that art justify its existence to win establishment approval. “All activity is vain,” declared poet Tristan Tzara in his 1918 “Dada Manifesto,” including the “monetary system, pharmaceutical product, or a bare leg advertising the ardent sterile spring…. The beginnings of Dada were not the beginnings of art, but of disgust” with the ossified culture of the “nice, nice bourgeois,” who would preserve at any cost “the possibility of wallowing in cushions and good things to eat.” “And so Dada,” wrote Tzara, “was born of a need for independence, of a distrust toward unity.” Such declarations aside, the movement was decidedly unified in its aims. “For us, art is not an end in itself,” poet Hugo Ball wrote. “It is an opportunity for the true perception and criticism of the times we live in.” This critique required new experimental techniques that deformed and repurposed the technologies of mass culture. cards.source_text: Image by Library of Congress/Carl Van Vechten, via Wikimedia Commons Many a foreigner has visited England and found it an unexpectedly surreal place. Some of that effect has to do with encountering familiar icons — Big Ben, double-decker Routemaster buses, Marmite — in cold, damp reality. More of it may be induced by the country’s simultaneously thoroughgoing cultures of normality and eccentricity, an endless source of inspiration for Monty Python’s Flying Circus and much other British comedy since. Yet England came relatively late to Surrealism, or rather, Surrealism came late to England. When the International Surrealist Exhibition opened at the New Burlington Galleries behind London’s Royal Academy in the summer of 1936, the Manchester Evening News decried it as “a travesty of everything that’s decent.” Naturally, the show was a smash hit. On display was work by artists including Pablo Picasso, René Magritte, Max Ernst, Alexander Calder, Giorgio de Chirico, Marcel Duchamp, Alberto Giacometti, Paul Klee, Man Ray, and Salvador Dalí, who turned up in person to deliver a lecture on “Authentic Paranoiac Phantoms.” In order to “descend to the subconscious” with a properly Surrealist literalism, he rented a diving suit and helmet from a local outfitter for his appearance. Pelee sits at the nexus of two important migration routes, making it a destination for birds travelling thousands of kilometres each year. Ravens are not among its regular visitors – only one was spotted in recent memory, in 2023 – but Atwood likes the old Inuit joke about them. A hunter arrives at a place he has never camped before, and asks a raven where to spend the night. “The raven says, ‘The base of that hill is a good place,’ and so he sets up his little tent there,” says Atwood. “In the middle of the night, a boulder rolls down the hill and crushes him. And the raven, as he’s enjoying the feast, says, ‘Works every time.’” The bestselling Canadian author, whose prophetic works of speculative fiction have won countless awards, has blurred the lines that separate humans and birds both in her work and, at times, in her life. She and Gibson, also a novelist, once dressed up for a party as Odin’s ravens, Thought and Memory. They wore black gloves and fashioned beaks from black construction paper. Gibson died in 2019. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 29 minute listen Forty iron rectangles, each one blunt as a piano key, rotate into a blurring fury that hides the eight-foot-long shaft at the heart of the flail chopper. I am perched atop several tons of iron, with 80 horsepower at my command. This part of farming is straightforward – even a mechanically challenged tree-hugger like me can manage to depress the clutch, shift into second, and ease the throttle forward. The tractor’s tall, deeply treaded tires churn, revolving into a smooth spin. Everything is spinning: fans, belts, alternator, the driveshaft, axles. I don’t understand the mechanism fully, yet the tractor and chopper and I are propelled forward across the knee-high whiskers of a coarsely bearded cornfield. It is Indian summer in southern Wisconsin. My wife and I and our young son live here on her family’s farm. Both of us are employed off the farm, but on weekends and many evenings I am an apprentice to my father-in-law, David. Today, we are taking advantage of a brief period of warm, dry weather. Winter is approaching, and I could be spending the day beside our woodsplitter – the gasoline-sipping, hydraulically heroic mechanism that makes it possible to put up several cords of firewood quickly each year – but that work can wait until the cool, sunny days of fall are shoved aside by the relentless spin of the earth into darkness, sleet, snow and frozen ground. The wall of tall green corn that stood here this summer has been transformed by fall and harvest. Little is standing after the field was stripped by a seed-combing combine. The mechanical tornado flails so loudly behind me: wailing against the air, grinding off the root-buttressed corn-stalk stumps, sucking up spent leaves and stripped cobs. In my wake, dry corn litter passes through the chopper like water compelled into frothy turbulence, falling again into an even, silent surface that hides so much activity below. cards.source_text: When the speakers are throbbing and rattling, spitting a filthy squeal, threatening to split open—do you bolt out of the room or step closer? If you ever attend a Gilla Band show, you will know instantly which their fans prefer. Discomfort is the baseline goal for a band that weaponizes its instruments to such earsplitting magnitudes that they rarely resemble the tried tools of rock music: guitar, bass, drums. “The trick,” bassist Daniel Fox said in a recent interview with Pitchfork, “is to be louder than everyone else.” This is a wild but typical understatement from the humble Irish quartet, which also comprises vocalist Dara Kiely, guitarist Alan Duggan Borges, and drummer Adam Faulkner. Volume—blown out to extremes or dampened before a deafening blast—in no way explains Gilla Band’s precision as songwriters, producers, or engineers. What may sound like chaos is the product of meticulous layering and sonic manipulation that smudges the lines between post-punk, noise, no wave, industrial, and techno. On their exhilarating fourth album, Pugnello, Gilla Band sharpen their implements and go in for the kill. Sure, Pugnello is loud, but it’s the nasty textures, the colliding rhythms, the gnarled vocals, the dense details that affirm Gilla Band’s mastery of dissonance. It’s their most methodical and charged album to date. Not long after they formed in 2011, Gilla Band began experimenting with a bracing concoction of noise-punk and dance music. In 2013, they released “Why They Hide Their Bodies Under My Garage,” a cover of the post-dubstep single by English DJ Blawan. The original simmers for six minutes at a steady pace and decibel level; Gilla Band stretch it, torque it, and spike it with pedal-warped guitar that sounds more like a feat of extreme knob-wringing. Watching them perform it live is a study in tension and release, dynamics they wield like classical conductors or spring break DJs. Gilla Band withhold the drop for a torturous length of time, whipping the crowd into a frenzy of potential energy. Just before they kick up the volume and crash-land on the beat, they pull back to near silence, a single fret slide bridging the gap. cards.source_text: My generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. Some of us are wounded: Salman Rushdie by an attacker’s knife, Julian Barnes lives with blood cancer, others with the fatal hurt of being forgotten. But what’s the likely fate of those of us who are surviving – for now? Do readers still love us? When Barnes announced that he was signing off because of illness, was he also intuiting that the younger generations had heard enough from us old birds and geezers who were young when Sean Connery had dimples, when David Hockney first coloured his hair yellow? The answer is probably “yes”. But here’s what I believe: contrary to what publishers hope and expect, serious writers don’t think obsessively about readers, or even about sales, royalties and prizes. What we talk to each other about, what we dream of, what we can’t live without is the work itself. When I endured a terrifying procedure for pancreatic cancer in 2019 and contemplated the likelihood of dying in Addenbrooke’s hospital, I spent wide-awake nights mourning not only the people I love and the places that are precious to me, but the end of storytelling. Ideas for stories have peopled my life since the age of 12, when I wrote my first play at boarding school. My existence devoid of these would definitely feel what Amis once called “thin”. From interviews Hockney gave towards the end of his 88 years, when yellow had turned to white, we gleaned a fine understanding of the elderly artist’s unflagging commitment to a day-by-day engagement with his art. The simplicity of the Hockney philosophy – “I wake up. And I go to work” – enabled him to rival Picasso with the vastness and variety of his output. He lived and breathed painting. The idea that he would suddenly stop doing this he would surely have thought plain stupid, and I’m with him on that. Though there can be a falling-off in the work of artists and writers as they age, this is by no means inevitable; the reasons for keeping on are not too hard to find. Certainly I’m getting towards the end of my life, but why should what remains of it be stricken by the loss of the one constant that has kept me company for 70 years, since that first little school play? Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman. But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam. Michael Cragg’s illuminating new book explores Kylie’s multiple selves, her talent for shapeshifting, and the question of why she has been persistently underrated. He makes the case that the most easily maligned aspects of her music – frivolity without subtext, fun without an underlying seriousness – are precisely what makes it so pleasurable and available for camp reclamation, its apparent disposability capable of being recast as a virtue. The Aussie girl next door is thus a different kind of gay icon to club kid Madonna, a grittier figure who looms large here, and whose own acts of reinvention have been considered not just the work of an entertainer, but of an auteur. This comparison is also a matter of taste, of course; in a particularly juicy quote included in the chapter on Kylie’s appeal among gay audiences, singer Rufus Wainwright describes her “as the anti-Madonna. Foley makes a commendable attempt, removing Miss Marple from the postwar austerity of St Mary Mead to the comparative luxury of the Swiss Alps. Although we are introduced to the unnamed body in the gondola cabin at the start, an immediate backward shift for a two-day lead-up means Miss Marple has little actual detecting to do until about halfway through the proceedings. Employing four narrators rather dilutes things, as well as necessitating a considerable amount of Murder of Roger Ackroyd-style withholding of information, but Foley’s Miss M shows her true colours when – of course – the hotel gets cut off from the outside world, and provides a solution worthy of the Queen of Crime herself. All we know at the start is that “a brutal murder was committed” and Hallett slowly but expertly ratchets up the tension as clashes over casting, power plays, marital suspicions and distrust of newcomers create an entire gallery of potential murderers and murderees. cards.source_text: Pursuing sex and love as a highly accomplished and beautiful woman—a baddie—is hard work. People will call you conceited simply for having high standards, partners might act intimidated or jealous of your success, and what about the guys you’ll have to beat off with a stick when they get too attached? Such are the problems Jae Stephens confronts on her stellar major label debut, AUDACITY. Born in Dallas and raised in Los Angeles, Stephens is a Beyoncé Tumblr stan turned self-taught pop artist. She found early success as a songwriter, helping to pen tracks for the likes of Normani, Ashanti, and Jennifer Lopez, but she’s been releasing music under her own name since 2017. On 2024’s SELLOUT EP, she hit her stride with flirty, neotraditional tracks that nodded to the rhinestone shine of 2000s-era radio R&B and established her persona as an ultra-confident, playfully misandrist diva. AUDACITY speaks boldly about relationships in the voice of a woman who isn’t embarrassed to say that she’s the prize. No score yet, be the first to add. Stephens is a pop student in a way that a former stan would be, and AUDACITY reads from an encyclopedia of acclaimed Black pop artists and producers: the percussive snap of opener “Crush” recalls Janet Jackson’s new-jack-swingy “Nasty.” “Gymnastics” and “Expensive & Difficult” feel closer to Timbaland’s shuddering pop production of the 2000s and the distorted dancefloor blur of Danja’s work on Blackout. Ashanti’s “Foolish” and Willow’s “Whip My Hair” both get name-checked on “B4U.” “I Miss the City” features a blinging harp melody akin to Brandy’s “All in Me,” produced by Darkchild. She may have grown her bawdy style and pop star image through fandom, but Stephens brings her own brazen personality and winking, trollish humor. Songwriting, she recently told Rolling Stone, is “the one place I’m allowed to be the villain. I’m allowed to say what I want, and the listener can decide if I’m serious or not.” On “Expensive and Difficult,” she sings that she likes “bringing home the bacon/But I’ll still spend yours, that’s reparations.” She’s practically training sexual partners like show dogs on songs like “Attaboy!” and “Sugar Trap,” but she’s not always as tough as she talks. In the album’s softer moments, Stephens sings about conflict and vulnerability without breaking character. items.title: ‘My generation of novelists is dying’: Rose Tremain on 70 years of writing, and late-life inspiration
items.summary: As her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stop My generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. Some of us are wounded: Salman Rushdie by an attacker’s knife, Julian Barnes lives with blood cancer, others with the fatal hurt of being forgotten. But what’s the likely fate of those of us who are surviving – for now? Do readers still love us? When Barnes announced that he was signing off because of illness, was he also intuiting that the younger generations had heard enough from us old birds and geezers who were young when Sean Connery had dimples, when David Hockney first coloured his hair yellow? items.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
items.summary: Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley; The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett; Cold Sunset by William Boyd; The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson and The Last Tenant by Eva Björg Ægisdóttir Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, £22) This, the first Miss Marple continuation novel, must have been a more difficult undertaking than a new Hercule Poirot; furnished by Christie with a cartoonist’s worth of exaggerated traits, the Belgian detective is surely easier to bring off the page than the unassuming but observant elderly spinster. Foley makes a commendable attempt, removing Miss Marple from the postwar austerity of St Mary Mead to the comparative luxury of the Swiss Alps. Although we are introduced to the unnamed body in the gondola cabin at the start, an immediate backward shift for a two-day lead-up means Miss Marple has little actual detecting to do until about halfway through the proceedings. Employing four narrators rather dilutes things, as well as necessitating a considerable amount of Murder of Roger Ackroyd-style withholding of information, but Foley’s Miss M shows her true colours when – of course – the hotel gets cut off from the outside world, and provides a solution worthy of the Queen of Crime herself. items.title: Can’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius?
items.summary: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon ‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman. But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam.
